text: , use simple example illustrate performance difference lstrrr.
code: files <- list.files(all.files = TRUE, recursive = TRUE) files_list <- dir_listwise(files) slow_string_op <- function(x, n = 10) {   stopifnot(is.character(x))    out <- x    for (i in seq_len(n)) {     out <- paste0(       rev(strsplit(out, "", fixed = TRUE)[[1]]),       collapse = ""     )     out <- toupper(out)     out <- tolower(out)   }    out }  set.seed(123)  bench_map <- microbenchmark::microbenchmark(   purrr_10 = {     purrr::walk(files, \(x) slow_string_op(x))   },   lstrrr_10 = {     list_walk(files_list, \(x) slow_string_op(x))   },   rrapply_10 = {     rrapply::rrapply(files_list, f = \(x) slow_string_op(x))   },   purrr_50 = {     purrr::walk(files, \(x) slow_string_op(x, n = 50))   },   lstrrr_50 = {     list_walk(files_list, \(x) slow_string_op(x, n = 50))   },   rrapply_50 = {     rrapply::rrapply(files_list, f = \(x) slow_string_op(x, n = 50))   }   # ,   # purrr_100 = {   #   purrr::walk(files, \(x) slow_string_op(x, n = 100))   # },   # lstrrr_100 = {   #   list_walk(files_list, \(x) slow_string_op(x, n = 100))   # },   # rrapply_100 = {   #   rrapply::rrapply(files_list, f = \(x) slow_string_op(x, n = 100))   # } ) print(bench_map) #> Unit: milliseconds #>        expr       min        lq      mean    median        uq      max neval #>    purrr_10  3.615778  3.706007  4.726053  3.756296  3.806342 61.40171   100 #>   lstrrr_10  3.529089  3.635877  3.989060  3.676284  3.716994  9.00946   100 #>  rrapply_10  3.590120  3.682322  3.950555  3.739477  3.785840 13.84159   100 #>    purrr_50 17.239350 17.682814 18.483424 17.868550 18.007398 32.69678   100 #>   lstrrr_50 17.329775 17.686205 18.905134 17.840725 18.186308 24.78150   100 #>  rrapply_50 17.108436 17.723896 18.865973 17.894264 18.224511 23.06341   100 ggplot2::autoplot(bench_map) +   ggplot2::theme(axis.text = ggplot2::element_text(size = 12)) #> Warning: `aes_string()` was deprecated in ggplot2 3.0.0. #> ℹ Please use tidy evaluation idioms with `aes()`. #> ℹ See also `vignette("ggplot2-in-packages")` for more information. #> ℹ The deprecated feature was likely used in the microbenchmark package. #>   Please report the issue at #>   <https://github.com/joshuaulrich/microbenchmark/issues/>. #> This warning is displayed once per session. #> Call `lifecycle::last_lifecycle_warnings()` to see where this warning was #> generated.

title: Use lstrrr to do some purrr-like things
text: Let’s use build-dataset sputnik_1 example:  can use list_flatten() flatten nested list flattened list (elements list nested):   names elements dot-separated paths elements:  Separation symbols can customized. Generally don’t recommend using _ purrr , ’s common separator names.  Recursive mapping main difference lstrrr::list_flatten() purrr::list_flatten()., former flatten levels list, latter flatten second level list (first level list ).
code: list_nleaf(sputnik_1) v <- list_flatten(sputnik_1) head(v, 3) cli::cli_alert_info("Class of v: {.cls {class(v)}}") cli::cli_alert_info("Length of v: {.val {length(v)}} (using {.fun length})") cli::cli_alert_info(   "Length of v: {.val {list_nleaf(v)}} (using {.fun list_nleaf})" ) head(names(v)) v2 <- list_flatten(sputnik_1, "$") head(names(v2)) v3 <- purrr::list_flatten(sputnik_1, is_node = is.list) head(v, 3) cli::cli_alert_info("Class of v3: {.cls {class(v3)}}") cli::cli_alert_info("Length of v3: {.val {length(v3)}} (using {.fun length})") cli::cli_alert_info(   "Length of v3: {.val {list_nleaf(v3)}} (using {.fun list_nleaf})" )

title: Use lstrrr to do some purrr-like things
text: lstrrr provides set functions similar purrr’s, handling nested lists. Just use list_* prefix function name.   want map multiple lists, make sure lists structure.   Customize progress bar:  list_find() used find elements satisfy predicate. Please note result list 1 level.  list_find_value() used find paths element identical given value. Unlike list_find(), matches predicate, list_find_value() matches value using identical() semantics.  list_filter() used filter leaves satisfy predicate. Unlike list_find(), returns flat list matches, list_filter() keeps original nested structure replaces non-matching leaves NULL.  list_modify_if used modify elements satisfy predicate. structure list preserved.
code: foo <- list(a = 1, b = list(c = "a", d = FALSE))  list_map(foo, \(x) typeof(x)) |> str() list_imap(foo, ~ paste(.y, ":", .x)) |> str() list_walk2(foo, foo, ~ message(paste0(.x, .y))) list_pwalk(   list(foo, foo, foo),   \(x, y, z) {     Sys.sleep(0.5)   },   .progress = "pwalk" ) list_walk(   sputnik_1,   ~ Sys.sleep(0.05),   .progress = list(name = "foo", type = "download") ) list_find(foo, ~ is.character(.x)) |> str() x <- list(   a = 1,   b = list(c = 2, d = list(e = 1)),   list(1) )  list_find_value(x, 1) |> str() list_filter(foo, is.numeric) |> str() list_modify_if(foo, is.logical, ~ !.x) |> str()

what: Functional Tools for Working with Complex and Deeply Nested R Lists
title: Functional Tools for Working with Complex and Deeply Nested R Lists
text: lstrrr provides functional programming tools working deeply nested R lists — path-based access, recursive mapping/walking, conditional modification, structure visualization. Motivation comes purrr purrr can handle R list, converts R list vector atomic, want. lstrrr designed work R list return list structure.

title: Functional Tools for Working with Complex and Deeply Nested R Lists
code: # install.packages("pak") pak::pak("Exceret/lstrrr")

title: Functional Tools for Working with Complex and Deeply Nested R Lists
text: Use just like purrr
code: library(lstrrr)  x <- list(   a = 1,   b = list(x = 2, y = list(i = 3, j = 4)) )  # Path-based access list_get(x, c("b", "y", "i")) #> [1] 3  # Recursive mapping list_map(x, ~ .x * 2) |> str() #> List of 2 #>  $ a: num 2 #>  $ b:List of 2 #>   ..$ x: num 4 #>   ..$ y:List of 2 #>   .. ..$ i: num 6 #>   .. ..$ j: num 8  # Flatten with path names list_flatten(x) |> str() #> List of 4 #>  $ a    : num 1 #>  $ b.x  : num 2 #>  $ b.y.i: num 3 #>  $ b.y.j: num 4  # Conditional modification (only values > 2) list_modify_if(x, ~ is.numeric(.x) && .x > 2, ~ .x * 10) |> str() #> List of 2 #>  $ a: num 1 #>  $ b:List of 2 #>   ..$ x: num 2 #>   ..$ y:List of 2 #>   .. ..$ i: num 30 #>   .. ..$ j: num 40  # Tree visualization (requires ggplot2) # viz_list(x)

title: Functional Tools for Working with Complex and Deeply Nested R Lists
text: similar project rlist, complex nested list. Let’s see work differently. code snippet rlist: nums becomes complex nested list, rlist may work expected. Recursive mapping main difference lstrrr rlist. lstrrr views list tree, recursively applies function leaf nodes. Another similar project rrapply, also provide list recursion R. differences lstrrr rrapply follows: lstrrr follows design philosophy purrr, whereas rrapply based base R’s rapply(). lstrrr provides native progress bar similar one purrr (using cli C API). lstrrr provides several basic functions working nested lists, list_set(), list_get(), list_nleaf(). see examples, click

chr [1:2] "min" "max" #>  $ b: Named num [1:2] 2 4 #>   ..- attr(*, "names")= chr [1:2] "min" "max" #>  $ c: Named num [1:2] 3 5 #>   ..- attr(*, "names")= chr [1:2] "min" "max" b: num 11 #>  $ c: num 15 nums <- list(   a = c(1, 2, 3),   b = c(2, 3, 4),   c = c(3, 4, 5),   d = list(     e = c(4, 5, 6),     f = c(5, 6, 7)   ) )  try(rlist::list.map(nums, c(min = min(.), max = what: Delete a nested element by path — list_delete
title: Delete a nested element by path — list_delete
text: Delete nested element path

title: Delete a nested element by path — list_delete
code: list_delete(x, path)

title: Delete a nested element by path — list_delete
text: x nested list traverse. Lists traversed recursively. Non-list objects treated leaves. Data frames traversed treated leaf values. path Character integer vector giving path retrieve. character path, component selects named element current level. integer path, component selects element position. Positional indices one-based, following normal R indexing conventions. path evaluated left right. example, c("b", "y", "") means x[["b"]][["y"]][[""]].

title: Delete a nested element by path — list_delete
text: modified copy x element path removed.

title: Delete a nested element by path — list_delete
code: x <- list(   a = 1,   b = list(     x = 1,     y = list(i = 1, j = 2)   ) )  list_delete(x, c("b", "y", "j")) #> $a #> [1] 1 #>  #> $b #> $b$x #> [1] 1 #>  #> $b$y #> $b$y$i #> [1] 1 #>  #>  #>   # Delete by integer path list_delete(x, c(2L, 2L, 1L)) #> $a #> [1] 1 #>  #> $b #> $b$x #> [1] 1 #>  #> $b$y #> $b$y$j #> [1] 2 #>  #>  #>   # The original object is unchanged unless reassigned x2 <- list_delete(x, c("b", "x")) names(x$b) #> [1] "x" "y" names(x2$b) #> [1] "y"
